Free focus tools

20 short exercises on focus, 2 to 14 minutes each, free and with no account needed. Open one and it runs right in the page.

The 20 tools

  • When your attention is sharpest

    Mark the times in your week when you can actually concentrate. Most people schedule their hardest work at their worst times without knowing it.

    Week map · 3 min

  • What pulls you away

    Sort your distractions into ones that come from outside, ones that come from inside, and ones that are both. Each kind wants a different fix.

    Sorter · 4 min

  • The conditions you focus best under

    Choose the conditions that genuinely help you concentrate. Not what productivity advice says; what has actually worked for you.

    Card pick · 4 min

  • The friction of getting started

    Rate how often a set of starting struggles has been true lately: circling a task, needing the perfect moment, finishing easy things to avoid the hard one.

    Reflection · 5 min

  • One thing for ten minutes

    A guided single-task session: choose one thing, set the conditions, work for ten minutes, then notice what happened in your attention.

    Guided exercise · 14 min

  • Where an hour actually goes

    Divide 100 points across what a typical working hour really contains: the task, the phone, messages, drifting, getting up, and finding your place again. Most people overestimate the first bar.

    Budget · 4 min

  • Clear or wanted

    Place tasks on a grid of how clear the next step is against how much you want to do them. Each corner stalls for a different reason and needs a different push.

    Grid · 6 min

  • Seven days of attention

    Each day, rate how easily you got started, how long your longest unbroken stretch felt, and how much of the day went where you meant it to. A week is more honest than any single day.

    7-day log · 2 min

  • Close one, open the next

    Four slow breaths to close one task before opening the next. Attention drags the last thing into the next thing unless you give it a moment to let go.

    Breathing · 2 min

  • Things you tell yourself about focus

    Turn over cards that show a familiar story about how you work on one side, and on the other a way to check whether it is true today, for this task.

    Perspective cards · 5 min

  • The last ten percent

    Rate how often a set of finishing struggles has been true lately: losing interest near the end, polishing instead of closing, leaving things almost done. Starting gets all the attention; finishing has its own friction.

    Reflection · 5 min

  • Signs your attention has already left

    Tick the tells you recognize from the moments when you are still at the task but no longer really on it. Catching these ten seconds earlier is most of the skill.

    Noticing list · 3 min

  • Coming back after an interruption

    A short guided routine for the minutes after someone or something breaks your concentration: mark where you were, close the intruder, settle, and re-enter without the usual long drift.

    Guided exercise · 6 min

  • Build your interruption plan

    Assemble defenses for the three sources of interruption: devices, people, and your own wandering mind. Each needs a different move, and they only work if you decide them in advance.

    Plan builder · 5 min

  • The order of your day

    Rank the kinds of work you do by when they belong in your day, from first thing to last. Most people put the easiest, most interrupting work first and wonder where the good hours went.

    Ranking · 4 min

  • What holds your attention, and what does not

    Set a dial for how easily you sink into different kinds of activity. Attention is not one thing; most people have a couple of activities where it comes free and a couple where it never does.

    Dials · 4 min

  • Reverse-engineer a good session

    Take apart a recent time when your attention actually held: what the task was, what got you in, what kept you there, what nearly broke it, and what you could copy on purpose.

    Guided writing · 8 min

  • The task under the distraction

    For the moment you catch yourself scrolling or wandering. Five quick prompts to name what you were supposed to be doing, what about it made you leave, and what would make the next five minutes possible.

    Guided writing · 4 min

  • Why tasks stall for you

    Sort everyday tasks by the reason they tend to stall for you: unclear, dull, or uncomfortable. Each reason has a different fix, and most people reach for the wrong one by default.

    Sorter · 5 min

  • Breaks that actually give something back

    Choose the breaks that genuinely restore your attention rather than quietly draining it. The difference is obvious in hindsight and nearly invisible at the time.

    Card pick · 4 min

What these tools are, and are not

Every tool here is free and works without an account: choose cards, move dials, sort a list, follow a paced breath, or keep a seven-day log, and read back what you noticed at the end. They are built to make a vague feeling more specific, which is often the first useful step.

None of them diagnoses, screens for or treats anything, and nothing you see at the end is a score or a label. If something you notice worries you, a licensed therapist is the right next conversation, and the directory is free to browse.
